why_text_based_first.argument: Recent systematic reviews report laboratory accuracies of 95-99% for CNN-based plant disease detection but field deployment accuracies of only 70-85%, a 15-30 percentage-point gap driven by lighting variation, background clutter, geographic bias in training data, and class imbalance. For smallholder contexts, the practical gap is wider still because RGB systems cost USD 500-2000 and hyperspectral systems USD 20,000-50,000, and most field models are uninterpretable to farmers. VRIKSHA-AI therefore prioritises a deterministic, explainable, text-and-context matching approach that works on any smartphone without a camera or internet connection. Image-based detection is planned as a clearly-labelled future phase in which a CNN output is treated as a triage signal fed into the same deterministic matcher, never as a standalone diagnosis.

image_integration_strategy.explanation: To prevent halluncinations and black-box misdiagnoses in agricultural advice, image classification models are used exclusively as a triage layer to extract candidate plant and disease labels. These labels are then evaluated by the deterministic context matcher against verified agricultural cases before generating any recommendation.

symptoms: Small soft-bodied insects clustered on the underside of leaves or tender shoots
Curling or yellowing of young leaves
Sticky honeydew residue on leaves, sometimes with black sooty mould developing on it
priority_actions: Inspect new growth and undersides of leaves 2-3 times a week during active growth.
Remove heavily affected leaves or shoots where practical and dispose of them off-site.
Conserve natural predators such as ladybird beetles and lacewings by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
Use the crop-specific validated option from the sustainable-approaches list below.
cases.modern_knowledge: Aphids (family Aphididae) are sap-sucking insects that reproduce rapidly in warm, humid conditions and cluster on tender new growth. They can transmit plant viruses, so early detection matters more than direct feeding damage.

sustainable_approaches.action: Use a strong jet of water to dislodge light infestations before considering any spray.
sustainable_approaches.availability: Universal - only requires water and a hose or sprayer.

sustainable_approaches.action: Encourage natural predators (ladybird beetles, lacewings, hoverflies) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides and planting flowering border plants.
sustainable_approaches.availability: Universal where flowering plants can be grown nearby.

sustainable_approaches.action: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which produces the soft growth aphids prefer.
Maintain airflow between plants to reduce the humid microclimate aphids favour.

principle.statement: Vrikshayurveda treats pest emergence as a symptom of imbalance in soil and plant vitality, not as an isolated problem to be attacked with a targeted poison.
principle.source_note: Team paraphrase of general principles; primary text is Surapala's Vrikshayurveda, trans. Sadhale (1996), Agri-History Bulletin No. 1, Asian Agri-History Foundation.

specific_practice.name: Kunapajala
specific_practice.description: A fermented liquid organic preparation made from animal or fish products boiled in water with paddy husk, sesame oilcake, black gram, milk, honey and ghee, then left to ferment for about a fortnight. Described in Surapala's Vrikshayurveda (verses 101-106) as a nourishing preparation for plant vitality. Used in modern practice as a soil or foliar application to support plant vigour and resistance.
specific_practice.primary_citation: Surapala's Vrikshayurveda, trans. N. Sadhale (1996). Agri-History Bulletin No. 1, Asian Agri-History Foundation, verses 101-106.
specific_practice.secondary_citation: Biswas, S. & Das, R. (2023). Kunapajala: A Traditional Organic Formulation for Improving Agricultural Productivity - A Review. Agricultural Reviews. doi:10.18805/ag.R-2570.
specific_practice.modern_evidence: Deshmukh, R.S., Patil, N.A., Nikam, T.D. (2012). Influence of Kunapajala treatment from Vrikshayurveda on the fruits of tomato under organic farming condition and its comparison with N.P.K. farming. Bioscience Discovery 3(2): 200-206. Also: Sarkar, S., Kundu, S.S., Ghorai, D. (2014). Validation of ancient liquid organics - panchagavya and kunapajala as plant growth promoters. Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 13(2): 398-403 (trials on tomato, chilli, cowpea).
specific_practice.evidence_level: Documented in primary Sanskrit text with modern peer-reviewed validation on this exact crop. Dose standardisation is still an open research area (Biswas & Das 2023).

iks_context.relevance_to_this_case: Kunapajala's role in strengthening plant vitality through soil and foliar nourishment is consistent with modern IPM's principle that reducing plant stress lowers aphid pressure. It is a plant-strengthening intervention, not a direct aphicide.
iks_context.verification_status: Principle is a team paraphrase. Kunapajala is directly cited to the primary text via Biswas & Das (2023). Team has not yet read verses 101-106 directly in the Sadhale translation; access is planned before final submission.

cases.connection: Modern pest monitoring and sustainable IPM (inspection, physical removal, predator conservation, airflow) are combined with the traditional plant-vitality approach of Vrikshayurveda, which treats pest emergence as a signal of soil and plant imbalance rather than an isolated problem.
cases.monitor: Observe new growth and pest activity 2-3 times per week for the next 7-10 days after the recommended action.
seek_expert_if: The infestation continues to spread across the plant within a few days.
Leaves show virus-like mottling (irregular yellow-green mosaic pattern).
The diagnosis remains uncertain after a week of observation.
The selected intervention does not produce the expected response.
cases.precautions: This is general agronomic and traditional context, not a confirmed diagnosis. Any spray or preparation should be tested on a small area first.
cases.expert_guidance: If the infestation spreads rapidly or leaves show virus-like mottling, consult a local agricultural extension officer or plant specialist promptly.

symptoms: Small dark brown or black circular spots on lower leaves, often with concentric rings
Yellowing around the spots
Spots progressing upward on the plant over time
priority_actions: Remove and dispose of affected lower leaves off-site (do not compost on-site).
Water at the base of the plant rather than overhead to keep foliage dry.
Increase spacing between plants to improve airflow.
Mulch around the base to reduce soil splash onto leaves.
cases.modern_knowledge: Leaf spot in tomato is commonly caused by fungal pathogens (e.g. Alternaria or Septoria species) that thrive in prolonged leaf wetness and warm, humid weather. It spreads through water splash and infected plant debris.

sustainable_approaches.action: Water at the base of the plant rather than overhead, to keep foliage dry.
sustainable_approaches.availability: Universal - only requires changing watering method.

sustainable_approaches.action: Remove and dispose of affected lower leaves off-site rather than composting on-site.
Increase spacing between plants to improve airflow and reduce leaf-wetness duration.
Mulch around the base to reduce soil splash onto leaves.
sustainable_approaches.availability: Straw, dry leaves, or crop residue available locally in most regions.

principle.statement: Traditional Indian plant-care practice places importance on soil health and drainage (Bhoomi Pariksha - soil assessment before cultivation) as a foundation for plant resistance, and documents periodic use of ash or plant-based preparations around the root zone as a preventive measure in humid seasons.
principle.source_note: Team paraphrase drawing on general Vrikshayurveda soil-assessment principles; primary text Surapala's Vrikshayurveda, trans. Sadhale (1996), Agri-History Bulletin No. 1, Asian Agri-History Foundation. The Bhoomi-Nirupanam sub-section on soil classification is described in Suresh et al. (2013).

specific_practice.name: Kunapajala (preventive application)
specific_practice.description: Kunapajala, described in Surapala's Vrikshayurveda (verses 101-106), is used in modern practice as a soil or foliar application to support plant vitality. In the leaf-spot context it is applied preventively rather than curatively, on the same Vrikshayurveda principle of maintaining plant vitality as a foundation for disease resistance.

specific_practice.secondary_citation: Biswas, S. & Das, R. (2023). Agricultural Reviews. doi:10.18805/ag.R-2570. Suresh, G. et al. (2013). Ancient Science of Life 33(1): 60-70.

iks_context.relevance_to_this_case: Kunapajala's traditional role as a soil and plant nourisher aligns with the modern principle that well-nourished, unstressed plants show greater resistance to fungal leaf-spot infections.
iks_context.verification_status: Principle is a team paraphrase of general soil-health principles. Kunapajala cited to primary text via Biswas & Das (2023). No specific Vrikshayurveda verse claims direct anti-fungal effect on tomato leaf spot - the application here is preventive, not curative.

cases.connection: Traditional emphasis on soil health and drainage (Bhoomi Pariksha) and periodic plant-vitality preparations (Kunapajala) is combined with modern fungal-disease prevention: keeping foliage dry, removing infected material, improving airflow, and mulching.
cases.monitor: Check lower leaves every 2-3 days for new spots. Watch for spot progression upward on the plant.
seek_expert_if: Spotting spreads to more than a third of the plant's foliage.
Spots appear on fruit.
The diagnosis remains uncertain after a week of observation.
The selected intervention does not produce the expected response.
cases.precautions: Fungal leaf spot can resemble other leaf diseases; exact identification may need visual confirmation of the spot pattern or a local expert's assessment.
cases.expert_guidance: If spotting spreads to more than a third of the plant's foliage or appears on fruit, consult a local agricultural extension officer for a targeted response.

symptoms: Older, lower leaves turning uniformly yellow
Slowed growth
Leaves not showing spots or insect presence
priority_actions: Check soil moisture 2-3 inches deep before watering, rather than watering on a fixed schedule.
Add composted organic matter gradually rather than a single large dose of fertilizer.
Check for root crowding if grown in a pot, and repot if roots circle the container base.
Observe whether yellowing starts from older or newer leaves, since this narrows the likely cause.
cases.modern_knowledge: General yellowing without spots or pests often points to a nutrient issue (commonly nitrogen), inconsistent watering, or root stress rather than a pest or pathogen. Diagnosis depends heavily on which leaves are affected and the surrounding pattern.

sustainable_approaches.action: Check soil moisture 2-3 inches deep before watering, rather than watering on a fixed schedule.
Add composted organic matter gradually rather than a single large dose of fertilizer.
sustainable_approaches.availability: Compost available on-site or locally in most regions.

sustainable_approaches.action: Check for root crowding if grown in a pot; repot if roots circle the container base.
sustainable_approaches.availability: Universal - larger pot and fresh potting mix.

sustainable_approaches.action: Observe whether yellowing starts from older or newer leaves - this narrows the likely cause.

principle.statement: Vrikshayurveda texts describe the practice of balanced, moderate watering and periodic organic nourishment to maintain steady plant vigour (Vriksha Ayush) and resistance to stress-related decline.
principle.source_note: Team paraphrase of general Vrikshayurveda nourishment principles; primary text Surapala's Vrikshayurveda, trans. Sadhale (1996).

specific_practice.name: Kunapajala (nourishment application)
specific_practice.description: Kunapajala, described in Surapala's Vrikshayurveda (verses 101-106), is the traditional fermented liquid organic preparation used for plant nourishment. In the yellowing context it is applied as a soil drench to restore plant vitality where nutrient or stress-related yellowing is suspected.
specific_practice.primary_citation: Surapala's Vrikshayurveda, trans. N. Sadhale (1996). Agri-History Bulletin No. 1, verses 101-106.
specific_practice.secondary_citation: Biswas, S. & Das, R. (2023). Agricultural Reviews. doi:10.18805/ag.R-2570.
specific_practice.modern_evidence: Deshmukh et al. (2012) and Sarkar et al. (2014) both report that Kunapajala application improved tomato plant vigour and leaf-level parameters (chlorophyll, leaf area, biomass) compared with NPK-only controls. This is directly relevant to a yellowing case.
specific_practice.evidence_level: Documented in primary text with modern replicated studies specifically on tomato vigour and leaf health.

iks_context.relevance_to_this_case: Kunapajala's documented effect on tomato leaf chlorophyll and vigour addresses the most common nutritional and stress-related causes of general yellowing.
iks_context.verification_status: Principle is team paraphrase. Kunapajala source citation is direct and exact. Modern evidence is specifically on tomato.

cases.connection: Traditional emphasis on balanced watering and periodic organic nourishment is combined with modern diagnostics: the leaf-age pattern (older vs newer) distinguishes nutrient from stress or root causes, and both traditional and modern approaches converge on gradual soil-improvement rather than a single corrective input.
cases.monitor: Check whether the yellowing progresses or stabilises over the next 2-3 weeks after adjusting watering and nutrition.
seek_expert_if: Yellowing continues despite consistent watering and nutrition over 2-3 weeks.
Yellowing appears on newer leaves rather than older leaves (suggesting a different nutrient or disease issue).
The diagnosis remains uncertain after 2 weeks of observation.
The selected intervention does not produce the expected response.
cases.precautions: Yellowing has many possible causes; this pathway narrows likely explanations but does not replace a soil or plant-tissue test where the cause is unclear.
cases.expert_guidance: If yellowing continues despite consistent watering and nutrition over 2-3 weeks, consult a local agricultural extension officer to check for root or soil-borne issues.

symptoms: White or grey powdery coating on leaves and buds
Distorted or curled new growth
Reduced flowering
priority_actions: Prune to open up the plant's centre and improve air circulation.
Avoid overhead watering in the evening, which raises humidity around foliage overnight.
Remove and dispose of heavily affected leaves and buds off-site.
Position new plantings with adequate spacing and morning sun exposure to dry dew quickly.
cases.modern_knowledge: Powdery mildew is a fungal disease that, unlike most fungal problems, thrives in dry conditions with high humidity at night and cool days with poor air circulation - not in standing water on leaves.

sustainable_approaches.action: Prune to open up the plant's centre and improve air circulation.
Avoid overhead watering in the evening; water in the morning at the base.
Remove and dispose of heavily affected leaves and buds off-site.
Position new plantings with adequate spacing and morning sun exposure to dry dew quickly.

principle.statement: Traditional Indian agricultural practice emphasises aligning cultivation, pruning, and planting activities with seasonal weather patterns (Ritu) to reduce exposure of tender growth to conditions that favour fungal development.
principle.source_note: Team paraphrase. General principle drawn from the Ayurvedic concept of Ritu (seasonal regimen) discussed in Singh et al. (2023); primary text reference is Vagbhata's Ashtanga Hridayam, Sutrasthana 3-4.

seasonal_principle.name: Ritu / Ritusandhi
seasonal_principle.description: In Ayurvedic literature the year is divided into six seasons (Ritu), each with distinct environmental characteristics and recommended practices. The transition between two seasons (Ritusandhi) is a 14-day period during which old-season practices are gradually phased out and new-season practices gradually introduced. The principle is one of gradual, timed adjustment to seasonal change.
seasonal_principle.source_citation: Vagbhata, Ashtanga Hridayam, Sutrasthana 3-4 (Ritucharya). Discussed in: Singh, N., Potter, B.S., Gupta, N., Mangal, G., Kumbhar, A. (2023). A Concept: Significant Role of Ritu and Ritusandhi in Today's Perspective. IJCRT 11(6): g120-g124.
seasonal_principle.verification_status: IMPORTANT: The source literature discusses Ritu and Ritusandhi for human seasonal health (Ayurveda), not for plant pathology. The application to plant-care here is a team extension of a general seasonal-timing principle, not a direct plant-specific citation. This is disclosed for transparency.

iks_context.relevance_to_this_case: Powdery mildew severity varies sharply with temperature and humidity transitions between seasons. The Ritu principle of gradual adjustment to seasonal change aligns with the modern practice of pruning and positioning plants to match seasonal weather conditions.
iks_context.verification_status: Principle is team paraphrase. Seasonal principle directly cited but is a team extension from human Ayurvedic Ritucharya to plant care - this is disclosed openly and not overstated.

cases.connection: Traditional seasonal-timing principles (Ritu) align with modern understanding that powdery mildew severity is driven by specific temperature and humidity transition conditions, and that pruning and positioning to match seasonal patterns reduces disease pressure.
cases.monitor: Check new growth weekly for powdery coating. Pay particular attention during seasonal transitions (early winter, early spring).
seek_expert_if: Mildew returns repeatedly across seasons despite pruning and spacing changes.
New growth is heavily distorted or flowering stops entirely.
The diagnosis remains uncertain.
The selected intervention does not produce the expected response.
cases.precautions: Powdery mildew severity varies significantly by rose variety; some are far more resistant than others, which this general pathway does not account for.
cases.expert_guidance: If mildew returns repeatedly across seasons despite pruning and spacing changes, consult a local nursery or horticulture expert about variety resistance.

Curled or distorted young leaves
Tiny slender insects visible on close inspection of flowers or leaf undersides

symptoms: White, cottony masses on bark, twigs or flower panicles
Sticky honeydew and sooty mould on affected parts
Ants actively moving along the trunk (they farm mealybugs for honeydew)
priority_actions: Apply a sticky band (grease band) around the trunk base before flowering to block upward movement.
Encourage natural predators such as the mealybug ladybird beetle.
Maintain clean basins around the trunk, removing fallen leaves and debris where eggs can overwinter.
Avoid excessive nitrogen application, which encourages the soft growth mealybugs prefer.
cases.modern_knowledge: Mealybugs are sap-sucking insects that often climb from the soil onto the trunk during flowering season and cluster on tender growth and flower panicles, potentially reducing fruit set.

cases.modern_knowledge: Brown spot in rice (Bipolaris oryzae) is strongly linked to nutrient-deficient soil (especially potassium) and water stress, alongside humid conditions; it is considered an indicator of overall crop and soil health rather than a purely weather-driven disease.

symptoms: Yellow striping along leaf veins, or general yellowing of lower leaves
Stunted growth in patches across the field
No visible insect presence
priority_actions: Check field drainage first, since waterlogged patches often show yellowing before the rest of the field.
Apply nitrogen in split doses matched to growth stage rather than a single large application.

Monitor specifically for yellow rust's characteristic powdery yellow stripe pattern.
cases.modern_knowledge: Yellowing in wheat without pest presence is commonly linked to nitrogen deficiency, waterlogging, or (if striped and patchy) yellow rust disease, which needs to be distinguished carefully since the response differs.

sustainable_approaches.action: Check field drainage first, since waterlogged patches often show yellowing before the rest of the field.
Apply nitrogen in split doses matched to growth stage rather than a single large application.

principle.statement: Traditional Indian agricultural practice emphasises aligning cultivation and field management activities with seasonal weather patterns (Ritu) to maintain crop resilience through changing conditions.
principle.source_note: Team paraphrase. General principle from the Ayurvedic Ritu concept as discussed in Singh et al. (2023).

seasonal_principle.name: Ritu / Ritusandhi
seasonal_principle.description: In Ayurvedic literature the year is divided into six seasons (Ritu), each with distinct environmental characteristics and recommended practices. The transition (Ritusandhi) between two seasons requires gradual adjustment of cultivation practices. For a winter crop like wheat, this principle applies to the adjustment of irrigation, sowing, and field management across the cool-to-warm transition.
seasonal_principle.source_citation: Vagbhata, Ashtanga Hridayam, Sutrasthana 3-4 (Ritucharya). Discussed in: Singh, N., Potter, B.S., Gupta, N., Mangal, G., Kumbhar, A. (2023). IJCRT 11(6): g120-g124.
seasonal_principle.verification_status: IMPORTANT: The source literature discusses Ritu for human seasonal health (Ayurveda), not plant pathology. The application to wheat field management here is a team extension of a general seasonal-timing principle, not a direct plant-specific citation.

iks_context.relevance_to_this_case: Wheat yellowing is influenced by temperature, water, and seasonal transitions. The Ritu principle of gradual, timed field management across seasonal change aligns with the modern drainage-first and split-nitrogen approach to wheat yellowing diagnosis.
iks_context.verification_status: Principle is team paraphrase. Seasonal principle directly cited but is a team extension from human Ayurvedic Ritucharya to plant care - disclosed openly.

cases.connection: Traditional seasonal-timing principles (Ritu) align with modern drainage-first and stage-matched nitrogen management in wheat, both responding to the same underlying principle that crop resilience depends on gradual, well-timed adjustment to changing conditions.
cases.monitor: Scout the field weekly. In particular, monitor drainage-affected patches and any yellow-rust-like striping. Re-check after nitrogen split application.
seek_expert_if: Yellowing shows a distinct powdery orange-yellow stripe pattern (suggesting rust).
Yellowing spreads rapidly across the field.
The diagnosis remains uncertain after 1-2 weeks of observation.
The selected intervention does not produce the expected response.
cases.precautions: Distinguishing nutrient yellowing from yellow rust disease is important since they need different responses; a close look at the pattern (striping vs. general) is the key differentiator.
cases.expert_guidance: If yellowing shows a distinct powdery orange-yellow stripe pattern, consult a local agricultural expert promptly, since rust can spread quickly across a field.

symptoms: Tiny white insects that fly up in a cloud when the plant is disturbed
Yellowing and curling of leaves
Sticky honeydew and sooty mould buildup
priority_actions: Use yellow sticky traps for early monitoring and population reduction.

Avoid dense planting that restricts airflow and creates a favourable whitefly microclimate.
Remove and destroy plants showing virus-like mosaic symptoms early to reduce spread.
cases.modern_knowledge: Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) are sap-sucking insects highly active in hot, humid weather and are a known vector for yellow vein mosaic virus in okra, making early population control more important than the direct feeding damage.

sustainable_approaches.action: Use yellow sticky traps for early monitoring and population reduction.

specific_practice.description: Kunapajala, described in Surapala's Vrikshayurveda (verses 101-106), is the traditional fermented liquid organic preparation used for plant nourishment. In the whitefly context it is applied as a plant-vitality intervention on the principle that stressed plants are more vulnerable to whitefly pressure and virus transmission.
